title: Updating Objects and Arrays in State

contentBlocks.body:
Treat state as **read-only**. React detects changes by reference: if you mutate an object and pass the same object back to the setter, `Object.is(old, next)` is true and React skips the render. Mutation also corrupts anything that kept the old value, such as an undo history or the previous props a memoized child compares against.

The fix is to create a new object or array for every level you change, and reuse (share) everything you did not change.

Array methods fall into two groups:

- **return new arrays** (safe): `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`, spread, and the newer `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `with`
- **mutate in place** (avoid on state): `push`, `pop`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`, and assigning `arr[i] = x`

For deeply nested state, consider flattening it (normalising by id) so each update touches fewer levels. Libraries such as Immer let you write mutating-looking code that produces immutable copies, but the rule underneath is the same.
`const next = state; next.items.push(item); setState(next);` does nothing visible: `next` is the same object, so React sees no change. It is one of the most common "my UI does not update" bugs.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why does items.push(newItem); setItems(items); not re-render?

choices: It passes the same array reference, so Object.is sees no change
Arrays cannot be stored in state
payload.answer: It passes the same array reference, so Object.is sees no change
payload.explanation: React compares by reference. Mutating and passing back the same array looks like no change.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Which call returns a new sorted array without mutating the original?

payload.explanation: toSorted (ES2023) returns a new array. sort and reverse mutate in place; splice mutates and returns the removed items.
